title: Eigentunes fold fractional tunes above 1/2 to 1 − ν
summary: `MATRIX_Lattice.getRingParametersDict` reports the eigentunes `fractional tune 1` and `fractional tune 2` as arccos(Re λ)/2π for two eigenvalues λ of the transverse one-turn matrix, and `TransferMatrixAnalysis.eigtunes` of the diagnostics package uses the same formula. The arccos range limits them to [0, 1/2], so a mode with fractional tune ν > 1/2 is reported as 1 − ν; the eigenvalues alone cannot distinguish the two, and neither method uses the eigenvectors that can. In an uncoupled four-cell FODO ring with plane tunes 0.4051 and 0.8812, both report eigentunes 0.4051 and 0.1188. The code's own uncoupled-ring test requires the eigentunes to equal the plane tunes and passes because its ring has fractional tunes below 1/2.

found.scope: source reading and a NumPy probe of the formula

title: `TEAPOT_MATRIX_Lattice.rebuild` raises KeyError for quadrupoles, multipoles and bends
summary: `TEAPOT_MATRIX_Lattice.rebuild(kin_energy)`, which remeasures the matrices at a new reference energy, tracks each recorded node with a parameter dictionary holding only the bunch and the node. The constructor also recorded the fringe-field child nodes, whose functions read `paramsDict["parentNode"]`, which only lattice traversal supplies, so rebuild raises KeyError: 'parentNode' at the first bend, or at the first quadrupole or multipole with a fringe field enabled, the default. A lattice of one quadrupole and one drift fails. A drift-only lattice, or a quadrupole with both fringe fields disabled, rebuilds and matches a fresh build at the new energy exactly.

title: `TEAPOT_MATRIX_Lattice` drops the feed-down of misaligned or off-orbit nonlinear elements
summary: `TEAPOT_MATRIX_Lattice` measures each node's transfer matrix from probe particles restarted on the reference axis before every node, so an orbit offset at a nonlinear element never enters its linearization. A sextupole of integrated strength K₂L displaced by (Δx, Δy) with the errors package, or on an orbit bump, loses its feed-down gradients K₂L·Δx and K₂L·Δy in the one-turn matrix, tunes and coupling, although the tracked map contains them. A thin sextupole with K₂L = 3 m⁻² displaced by (1.500, −0.900) mm has ∂x′/∂x = −4.500×10⁻³ m⁻¹ in the tracked map and 0 in the matrix lattice. In a FODO ring the matrix lattice reports the undisplaced tune 0.2698 where the tracked map has eigentunes 0.2676 and 0.2709. Linear misaligned elements are reproduced correctly.

title: A `BaseMATRIX` node with several parts applies its whole matrix in every part
summary: `BaseMATRIX.track` applies the node's full 7×7 transfer matrix M each time it runs, and lattice tracking runs it once per body part. A matrix node given N parts, for example to host child nodes between parts, therefore transports particles with Mᴺ, while `MATRIX_Lattice` builds its one-turn matrix, Twiss functions and tunes from M once. A 1 m drift matrix node with 2 parts moves a particle at x = 1 mm, x′ = 1 mrad to x = 3.000 mm, where the lattice's one-turn matrix and a TEAPOT drift give 2.000 mm. Matrix nodes built by `TEAPOT_MATRIX_Lattice` have one part and are unaffected.

title: The MAD-X reader repeats the previous statement for every line without a semicolon
summary: `TEAPOT_Lattice.readMADX` keeps the text of the last line that ended a statement and adds it again for every following line without a ';': blank lines, comments indented by a space and the first line of a statement that continues on the next line. A blank line or an indented comment after a sequence placement therefore places that element twice. A thin multipole with knl₁ = 0.01 followed by a blank line kicks a particle at x = 1 mm by Δpx = −2.000×10⁻⁵ instead of −1.000×10⁻⁵, with no message; a 1 m quadrupole followed by an indented comment appears twice and a 10 m sequence becomes 11 m long. A blank first line or a statement split over two lines stops the read with an exception.

title: `readMADX` turns every RFCAVITY into a drift
summary: `TEAPOT_Lattice.readMADX` changes the type of every RFCAVITY to a drift before the TEAPOT element factory sees it, so the imported lattice has no RF node: VOLT, LAG and HARMON are dropped with no message, and the ring has no longitudinal focusing or acceleration. MAD-X gives a particle crossing an RFCAVITY at the reference time the energy kick VOLT·sin(2π·LAG), with VOLT in MV. For `rf: rfcavity, l=1, volt=0.01, lag=0.25, harmon=1` an on-axis proton gains 0 instead of 1.000×10⁻⁵ GeV, and the cavity is a plain 1 m drift.

title: HKICKER and VKICKER lose their KICK strength on MAD and MAD-X import
summary: In MAD-X and MAD-8 the strength of an HKICKER or VKICKER is its KICK attribute, the change of px or py; only the two-plane KICKER uses HKICK and VKICK. The TEAPOT element factory reads only `hkick` and `vkick`, so through `readMADX` and `readMAD` every single-plane corrector defined with KICK is built with zero kick and no message. For `hk: hkicker, kick=0.001` and `vk: vkicker, kick=0.002` an on-axis particle leaves with px = py = 0 instead of 1.000×10⁻³ and 2.000×10⁻³. Correctors written with `hkick=` or `vkick=` import correctly.

title: A MAD-X MULTIPOLE with both KNL and KSL keeps only the array written last
summary: When a MAD-X MULTIPOLE gives both normal (KNL) and skew (KSL) integrated strengths, `readMADX` keeps only the array written last, with that array's normal or skew type, and drops the other with no message. MAD-X applies both: at y = 0 the quadrupole terms give a particle at x the kicks Δpx = −knl₁·x and Δpy = ksl₁·x. For `mp: multipole, knl={0, 0.1}, ksl={0, 0.05}` a particle at x = 1 mm leaves with Δpx = 0 instead of −1.000×10⁻⁴ and Δpy = 5.000×10⁻⁵; with KSL written first the skew kick is lost instead. Multipoles with a single array import correctly.

title: MAD-X attributes using asin, acos, atan, a name containing "pi" or a D exponent are set to zero
summary: `readMADX` rewrites `sin(` to `math.sin(` before it looks for `asin(`, so `asin(x)` becomes the invalid `amath.sin(x)`, and likewise for `acos` and `atan`; it also replaces every substring `pi`, so a variable named `kpip` becomes `kmath.pip`. Numbers with the exponent letter D, such as `1.5d-3` (0.0015 in MAD-X), are not translated at all. An element attribute written with such an expression cannot be evaluated, and the reader prints a warning, sets the attribute to 0 and builds the element. `k1=asin(0.5)` gives a quadrupole with k₁ = 0 instead of 0.5236 m⁻², and `k1=kpip` with `kpip = 0.2` gives 0 instead of 0.2000 m⁻². Expressions with `sin` and with `pi` itself evaluate correctly.

title: A MAD-X INSTRUMENT with length does not drift the beam
summary: `readMADX` imports an INSTRUMENT as a marker, which the TEAPOT element factory builds as a node without a tracking map. An instrument of nonzero length keeps its length, so element positions and the lattice length are right, but particles cross it without moving. In MAD-X an INSTRUMENT acts on the beam as a drift of its length. In a 10 m sequence holding a 2 m instrument, a particle with px = 1×10⁻³ leaves at x = 8.000×10⁻³ m instead of 1.000×10⁻² m. Monitors and collimators with length are drifted correctly.

title: MAD-X FROM= is measured from the reference point of the named element, not its centre
summary: In a MAD-X sequence, `AT=a, FROM=name` places an element at the distance a from the centre of the element `name`. `readMADX` adds a to the stored placement position of `name`, which is its entry or its exit when the sequence uses REFER=ENTRY or REFER=EXIT, so an element placed with FROM lands half the named element's length too early or too late. A marker at `AT=3, FROM=qa` after a 2 m quadrupole lands at 4 m instead of 5 m with REFER=ENTRY and at 6 m with REFER=EXIT. With the default REFER=CENTRE the position is right. For a name placed several times the reader measures from the latest earlier placement, where MAD-X uses the first.

title: The TEAPOT element factory stops on bare TILT flags, zero bend angles and RCOLLIMATOR
summary: Three valid MAD element definitions stop the TEAPOT lattice readers. A bend with ANGLE = 0 or without ANGLE, such as a field-free or pure-gradient sector magnet, raises ZeroDivisionError in `readMAD` and `readMADX` alike, because the bend's radius is computed as L/θ and the RBEND length conversion divides by sin(θ/2). A TILT without a value, which MAD-8 defines as the element's standard skew angle (π/4 for a quadrupole), raises AttributeError in `readMAD` for bends, quadrupoles, sextupoles and octupoles. RCOLLIMATOR, which the MAD-8 parser accepts, matches no factory branch because the factory tests for the misspelling "rcolimator", and the process exits with status 1.

title: The MAD-8 reader exits with status 0 on an unknown element type
summary: When `readMAD` meets an element type that is not in its list, it prints "There is no element with type" and ends the process with `sys.exit(0)`, the success status, without building a lattice. A batch job or test that reads a MAD-8 file with a misspelled type, or with a valid MAD-8 type the reader does not know, such as INSTRUMENT or ECOLLIMATOR, stops early but reports success. Reading a MAD-8 line with `q: quadrupol, l=1.0, k1=0.5` exits with status 0, and the statement after `readMAD` never runs. The MAD-X reader exits with status 1 for an unknown type, but with status 0 when a CALL statement names its file without quotes, which MAD-X accepts.

title: `readMADX` multiplies numbers written with a decimal point and an exponent by a power of ten
summary: `TEAPOT_Lattice.readMADX` misreads every number in an element attribute that has both a decimal point and an exponent: it takes `1.5e` in `1.5e-3` for a variable name, deletes its '.', and evaluates `15e-3`. The value is multiplied by 10 to the power of the number of digits after the point, with no message: `k1=1.5e-3` gives k₁ = 0.015 m⁻² instead of 0.0015 m⁻², and the MAD-X SAVE output `hkick:= -1.25e-05` gives a kick of −1.250×10⁻³ instead of −1.250×10⁻⁵. In a 16-cell ring saved by MAD-X with eight orbit correctors, the one-pass orbit reaches x = 24.93 mm instead of 1.156 mm. Integer mantissas, fixed-point decimals, variable definitions, AT positions and KNL/KSL arrays are read correctly.

title: MAD and MAD-X solenoid import applies the bunch charge to KS a second time
summary: `readMADX` and `readMAD` copy a SOLENOID's strength KS into the parameter `B` of a TEAPOT solenoid, whose map multiplies `B` by the bunch charge number q. MAD defines KS = B_s/(Bρ), with B_s the longitudinal field and Bρ the beam particle's rigidity, so its map is the same for every charge. The imported solenoid applies q·KS instead: antiprotons, electrons and H⁻ ions (q = −1) rotate the opposite way, and a q = 2 ion by twice the angle. For KS = 0.5 m⁻¹ over 1 m and a particle starting at x = 1 mm, q = −1 leaves at y = +0.2397 mm and q = +2 at x = 0.7702 mm, where MAD-X gives y = −0.2397 mm and x = 0.9388 mm.

title: MAD and MAD-X import reverses the sense of TILT
summary: `readMADX` and `readMAD` pass an element's TILT unchanged to the TEAPOT tilt nodes, whose rotation has the opposite sense to MAD's positive roll (x toward y), so every tilted element is built rolled by −TILT. A kicker with HKICK = 1 mrad and TILT = 0.4 kicks y′ by −0.3894 mrad where MAD-X gives +0.3894 mrad. A quadrupole with K1 = 0.5 m⁻² and TILT = 0.3 couples the planes with the wrong sign: a 3 m line from x = 1 mm, y = 2 mm ends at x = 1.280 mm instead of −0.4162 mm. A sector bend with TILT = π/2 disperses to −y instead of +y. Untilted elements, and tilted ones whose angle is negated after import, agree with MAD-X to 2×10⁻⁹ m.

title: `readMADX` drops the skew strengths K1S, K2S and K3S
summary: `TEAPOT_Lattice.readMADX` builds a QUADRUPOLE from K1 alone, a SEXTUPOLE from K2 alone and an OCTUPOLE from K3 alone, and discards their skew strengths K1S, K2S and K3S without a message. A skew quadrupole defined as `quadrupole, l=1, k1s=0.5` becomes a 1 m drift: from x = 1 mm, y = 2 mm a 3 m line ends at x = 1.000 mm instead of MAD-X's 2.555 mm, and a magnet with both K1 = 0.5 m⁻² and K1S = 0.2 m⁻² loses its coupling. A sextupole with L = 0.5 m and K2S = 6 m⁻³ gives no kick where MAD-X gives Δpx = 6.000 μrad. The same skew fields written as MULTIPOLE KSL arrays, and the normal strengths, agree with MAD-X.

title: `readMADX` imports a thin MULTIPOLE's dipole strength KNL[0] as an orbit kick on a straight reference
summary: In MAD-X a MULTIPOLE's dipole strength K0L = KNL[0] bends the reference trajectory like a thin bend of angle K0L: the design orbit is unchanged, and a particle with relative momentum deviation δ gets the dispersive kick K0L·δ. `readMADX` builds a TEAPOT multipole whose dipole term kicks every particle by Δx′ = −K0L on a straight reference, deflecting the design particle and omitting the dispersive term. Behind a 1 mrad thin multipole and 1 m of drift, a proton on the design orbit is at x = −1.000 mm, where MAD-X gives 0. In a thin-lens ring whose bends are such multipoles, as MAD-X MAKETHIN writes them, the design particle is 14.73 m off axis after one turn.

title: `trackBunch` leaves its tracking action in a caller's container after an exception, so the next call repeats every map
summary: When an action or a node raises inside `TEAPOT_Lattice.trackBunch`, `LinacAccLattice.trackBunch` or `trackDesignBunch`, or `AccNodeBunchTracker.trackBunch`, the temporary BODY action that applies each node's map stays in the caller's action container, because the method removes it only after a normal return. If the caller catches the exception and tracks again with that container, every node's map runs once more per earlier failure. For a 1 m drift and x′ = 10⁻³, x after one caught failure is 2.000×10⁻³ m instead of 1.000×10⁻³ m, and after three it is 4.000×10⁻³ m. Calls that let the method create its own container are unaffected.

title: `TEAPOT_Lattice.getSubLattice` rewrites the ring length of RF cavities in the original lattice
summary: `TEAPOT_Lattice.getSubLattice` builds a new lattice that shares its node objects with the original and initializes it, and `TEAPOT_Lattice.initialize` writes the lattice length into every `RingRFTEAPOT` node as its ring length C. Taking a sublattice that contains a ring RF cavity therefore changes the cavity in the original ring, whose RF kick qV·sin(2πhz/C) then uses the sublattice length. For a 100 m ring with a cavity after the first 10 m drift, `getSubLattice(0, 1)` changes the cavity's ring length from 100 m to 10 m, and the kick at z = 1 m grows from 6.279×10⁻⁵ GeV to 5.878×10⁻⁴ GeV. Calling `initialize()` on the original ring restores it.

title: Default tracking contexts persist across calls and lattices, so `path_length` and transport-matrix positions accumulate
summary: Seven tracking methods declare the context argument as `paramsDict={}`: `AccLattice.trackActions`, `AccNode.trackActions`, `AccNodeBunchTracker.trackBunch`, `TEAPOT_Lattice.trackBunch`, `MATRIX_Lattice.trackBunch`, `LinacAccLattice.trackActions` and `BaseLinacNode.trackDesignBunch`. Python creates each default dictionary once, so every call that omits the context continues from the `path_length` the previous call left, on any lattice. The linac transport-matrix controller positions its nodes through such a call: after a 3 m lattice, the matrix nodes of a 1 m lattice are placed at 3.0 and 3.5 m instead of 0.0 and 0.5 m. The linac aperture helpers' `aprtNodes=[]` default accumulates returned aperture nodes across lattices in the same way. The ordering of the matrix nodes and the matrices themselves are unaffected.

title: `RF_AxisFieldsStore` returns the first table read for a file name, from any directory and after the file changes
summary: `RF_AxisFieldsStore.addAxisField(file_name, dir_location)`, which `AxisFieldRF_Gap.readAxisFieldFile` and the axis-field gap replacement function call, caches each field table in a process-wide dictionary keyed by the file name alone. A later request for a file of the same name in another directory, or for the same file after it was rewritten, silently returns the first table read. Two lattices built in one process from field-map sets that share file names, such as two versions of a cavity's maps, both get the first set's fields. A file holding the constant field 2.0 in a second directory reads back as 1.0, and the first file rewritten with 7.0 still reads 1.0.

title: `AccNode` guard messages raise `TypeError` while being built, and a failed `setLength` leaves the node inconsistent
summary: Two guards of the base lattice node build their error message by concatenating an integer or a tuple to a string. Total `setLength()` on a node that has body children, and `addChildNode()` with an invalid placement code, therefore raise `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str` instead of printing the guard's explanation and stopping through `orbitFinalize`. `setLength` stores the new total before the guard runs, so a caller that catches the `TypeError` keeps a node whose length is 2.0 m while its parts still sum to 1.0 m. The sibling guard in `setnParts()` builds its message correctly and stops as intended.

title: `RF_AxisFieldsStore.addAxisFieldsForAccSeq` raises `NameError` on every call
summary: `RF_AxisFieldsStore.addAxisFieldsForAccSeq(accLattice, accSeqNamesList, dir_location)` loops over the undefined name `accSeqList` instead of its argument, so every call raises `NameError` before it reads any file, even for an empty list of sequence names. Its documented purpose, loading the axis fields of all RF gaps in the named sequences into the field store, is unavailable.

title: `RF_AxisFieldAnalysis` cannot analyse a two-gap cavity field and misplaces a single gap
summary: `RF_AxisFieldAnalysis`, which builds per-gap transit-time-factor tables from a cavity's axis field, takes the cavity center as the mean of the interior gap centers and divides their sum by the number of gaps minus two. For a two-gap field the default mode raises `ZeroDivisionError`, and the `zeroIsCenter=True` mode exits for any field with more than one gap, so two-gap cavities cannot be analysed. A one-gap field in the default mode divides by −1 and gets cavity center 0 instead of the gap center, so the gap position relative to the cavity center is 0.06000 m instead of 0 for a gap on [0, 0.12] m. Fields of three to five gaps get correct centers.

title: `BaseRF_Gap` documents the matrix gap model as its default, but the default is `RfGapTTF`
summary: The `BaseRF_Gap` class docstring says the matrix RF gap model is used by default and lists E₀TL and the mode as its parameters. The constructor installs `RfGapTTF`, the transit-time-factor model, which uses E₀L and the four transit-time-factor polynomials and ignores E₀TL. A gap configured as the docstring describes, with only E₀TL set, therefore gives no acceleration, because E₀L defaults to zero. For a 2.5 MeV proton with E₀TL = 0.1200 MeV at a cavity phase of −20°, the energy gain is 0 instead of qE₀TL·cos φ = 0.1128 MeV. Lattices from the SNS lattice factory set both E₀TL and E₀L and are unaffected.

title: Linac `Quad` accepts odd and negative part counts and divides by zero for none
summary: `Quad.initialize` states that a linac quadrupole needs an even number of parts, at least two, so that correctors can sit at its center. Its guard `nParts < 2 and nParts % 2 != 0` rejects only a single part: three, five or any other odd count is accepted, a negative count is accepted with an empty part list, and zero parts raise `ZeroDivisionError` instead of the intended message. The rejection message also loses its first sentence because a later assignment overwrites it.

title: `reverseOrder()` does not invert tilts, alignment errors, solenoid fields and hard-edge fringes
summary: `reverseOrder()`, the lattice reversal used for bunch backtracking, only swaps each node's entrance and exit children. An element tilted by a or displaced by Δx then runs its exit transform first and acts as tilted by −a or displaced by −Δx; a solenoid keeps its field B, although inverting its map needs −B; and a quadrupole or bend hard-edge fringe acts twice instead of cancelling. Backtracking, x′, y′ and z negated around tracking through the reversed lattice, therefore misses the start. At 100 MeV, a 0.5 m, 3 T/m linac quadrupole tilted by 0.3 rad returns a ray started at x = −0.2 mm with y′ off by 0.2293 mrad. Untilted quadrupoles and bend bodies return to the start within 10⁻¹⁸.

title: `SynchPartRedefinitionZdE.center_Z` doubles the bunch's mean z instead of removing it
summary: `SynchPartRedefinitionZdE.center_Z(bunch)` is documented to transform the synchronous particle's z to the bunch average, after which the bunch's mean longitudinal position ⟨z⟩ is zero. It passes +⟨z⟩ to `shift_Z`, which adds its argument to every particle's z, so ⟨z⟩ doubles instead. Three particles at z = 1, 2 and 3 mm end at 3, 4 and 5 mm instead of −1, 0 and 1 mm. The energy counterpart `center_dE` centers dE correctly, and `shift_Z(bunch, −⟨z⟩)` gives the centered bunch.

title: `LSpaceChargeCalc` and `LImpedance` apply the Fourier kick at z + z_c + Δz/2 instead of z
summary: `LSpaceChargeCalc` (default Fourier branch) and `LImpedance` bin the bunch on a grid of length C centred at the midpoint z_c of the bunch extrema, but reconstruct the kick with the phase 2πz/C + π, as if bin j were centred at −C/2 + jΔz, with Δz = C/N_b for N_b bins. A particle at z therefore receives the kick that belongs at z + z_c + Δz/2, and the kick changes when the bunch is shifted rigidly. In a 250 m ring with 128 bins, the space-charge kick on a Gaussian bunch with rms length 12.5 m deviates from the analytic kick by up to 12.84% of its peak when the bunch is centred at z = 0 and by 76.26% when centred at z = 5 m.

title: `LSpaceChargeCalc.setUseGrad(1)` scales the kick as q³ and reverses it for negative ions
summary: With `setUseGrad(1)`, `LSpaceChargeCalc` multiplies the binned line density by the charge number q and then by the classical radius r₀, which already contains q², so the energy kick scales as q³ instead of q² (one q for the source, one for the kicked particle). A negative ion (q = −1), such as H⁻, therefore gets a reversed kick and q = 2 a doubled one, while the default Fourier branch scales as q². For a Gaussian bunch in a 250 m ring, the gradient-branch kick at z = σ, in units of the analytic q = +1 kick, is −1.006 for q = −1 and 8.051 for q = 2, instead of +1 and 4.

title: `SpaceChargeCalc2p5Drb` takes the beam's vertical centre from the horizontal grid, so its energy kick depends on the transverse beam position
summary: `SpaceChargeCalc2p5Drb` scales its energy kick by G(r) = 1 + 2ln(b/a) − r²/a², with a the fitted beam radius, b the pipe radius and r the distance from the fitted beam centre, but it reads the vertical coordinate of each grid row from the horizontal grid. On a square grid with the default aspect ratio, the fitted vertical centre is therefore off by x_min − y_min, the difference of the two grids' lower limits, for centred beams too; other grids also scale the fitted vertical spread. For a round Gaussian beam with σ = 1.5 mm in a 20 mm pipe, a rigid 3 mm horizontal displacement changes the energy kicks by up to 32.84% of their peak and a 3 mm vertical one by 32.98%, instead of not at all.

title: `TImpedance` treats larger z as arriving later, so its multi-turn wake acts ahead of the source or with the wrong sign
summary: `TImpedance` builds its transverse kick from betatron sidebands n ± Q of θ = 2πz/C, with Q the tune and C the ring length, which is consistent only if larger z passes the impedance later. In PyORBIT larger z passes earlier (z = −β₀cΔt), so previous turns enter with the betatron phase of the wrong turn, and no impedance table makes the kick causal. With Chao-convention tables, as the upstream tests label theirs, the kick driven by the source's offset has the wrong sign; with engineering-convention tables the kick acts ahead of the source. For a resonator wake with 150 m memory the kicks deviate from the time-domain wake by 194.1% and 106.1% of its peak; on the z-mirrored bunch they match to 1.609%.

title: `SpaceChargeForceCalc2p5D` gives NaN, wrong kicks or a segmentation fault on grids with nx ≠ ny
summary: `SpaceChargeForceCalc2p5D(nx, ny, nz)` copies its Green function and multiplies the spectra in loops with interchanged x and y bounds, so only square transverse grids index its 2nx × 2ny arrays correctly. Rectangular grids give NaN, finite wrong kicks or a segmentation fault, depending on shape and memory contents. Inside a uniform round beam of radius a the kick is Δx′ = 2Lr₀λx/(β²γ³a²), with L the kick length, r₀ the classical radius and λ the line density. At x = a/2 a 64 × 64 grid gives 1.000 times this kick, a 64 × 63 grid 0.5314 times plus a spurious vertical kick of −0.5649 times, a 64 × 32 grid NaN, and a 32 × 64 grid crashes.

title: `Grid1D` smoothed gather centres its quadratic stencil on the lower node, so it jumps at every node
summary: `Grid1D.getValueSmoothed` and `calcGradientSmoothed` centre their three-point quadratic stencil on the grid node at or below z, so the offset f from the centre runs from 0 to 1 cell, but the weights ½(½ ∓ f)² and ¾ − f² form the quadratic B-spline only for |f| ≤ ½; the matching deposit `binValueSmoothed` uses the nearest node. The interpolant therefore jumps at node i by (gᵢ₊₁ − 3gᵢ + 3gᵢ₋₁ − gᵢ₋₂)/8, with gⱼ the grid values, 0.7500 for gⱼ = j³, and deposit and gather are not reciprocal. With `setUseGrad(1)` and `setSmoothGrad(1)`, `LSpaceChargeCalc` gives a symmetric Gaussian bunch (rms length 12.5 m, 128 bins over 250 m) a kick whose even part dE(z) + dE(−z) reaches 2.674% of the peak instead of zero.

title: `UniformEllipsoidFieldCalculator` gives a wrong field outside an elongated ellipsoid
summary: Outside a uniformly charged ellipsoid with semiaxes a, b, c, `UniformEllipsoidFieldCalculator` interpolates the field integral linearly in the confocal parameter λ from a 200-point table with spacing (2·max(a, b, c))²/199. For an elongated ellipsoid the transverse integral varies on the scale of the smallest semiaxis squared, far below that spacing, so the exterior field is wrong wherever λ is small against the step, near the surface and far away alike; the interior field is exact. The exact field is Fₓ = Q·x·R_D(c² + λ, b² + λ, a² + λ), with Q the charge and R_D Carlson's elliptic integral. For semiaxes (1, 1, 100) mm, Fₓ is 2.935 times exact at (1.5a, 0.5b, 0.4c) and 28.24 times at (4a, 3b, 0.5c).

title: `SpaceChargeCalcUnifEllipse(nEllipses > 1)` changes its field when weights are stored per particle or the bunch is displaced
summary: With more than one ellipsoid, `SpaceChargeCalcUnifEllipse` sorts particles into radial shells using raw, uncentred coordinates, with shell index int(nρ) − 1 for a scalar macro size but int(nρ) for a per-particle `macrosize` attribute, where n is the number of ellipsoids and ρ the normalized ellipsoidal radius. The same bunch therefore gets different fields when its identical weights are stored per particle or when it is displaced rigidly, and the scalar path itself misweights the shells. For a uniform ellipsoid, where a single ellipsoid gives the exact field, three ellipsoids give a core field of 1.038 times the exact value with a scalar macro size, 0.3135 times with the same weights stored per particle and 0.2138 times after a 3 mm horizontal displacement.

title: 2.5-D space charge wraps the bunch head's line density into its tail
summary: `SpaceChargeCalc2p5D` and `SpaceChargeCalc2p5Drb` fit the longitudinal grid exactly to the bunch extrema and deposit and interpolate the line density with the periodic linear stencil of `Grid1D`, so weight within half a bin of one end is shared with the bin at the other end. A particle near either end therefore receives a transverse kick scaled by a mixture of head and tail densities. For a uniform round beam whose line density rises linearly from zero at the tail, with 32 bins, a particle 0.4% of the bunch length from the tail gets 23.37 times the kick of the non-periodic binned density, one 0.4% from the head 0.6031 times, and a central one 0.9983 times. Flat-top profiles are unaffected.

title: `TImpedance` gives each particle the kick that belongs half a bin further along z
summary: `TImpedance` bins the bunch's transverse moments at cell centres z_min + (j + ½)Δz, with Δz = C/N_b for ring length C and N_b bins, but reconstructs the kick with the phase 2π(z − z_min)/C, which places bin j at its lower edge. Every sideband n ± Q, with Q the tune, is therefore shifted in phase by π(n ± Q)/N_b, and a particle at z receives the kick that belongs at z + Δz/2. For a symmetric, rigidly offset Gaussian bunch with rms length 10 m in a 248 m ring and one resistive sideband at Q = 6.23, the kick should be odd about the bunch centre, but K(z) + K(−z) reaches 2 sin(πQ/N_b) of the peak kick: 30.46% with 128 bins and 60.21% with 64.

title: A custom `Boundary2D` reports points outside its outline as inside
summary: A `Boundary2D(nPoints, nModes)` built from user points answers `isInside(x, y)` with a test against the bounding rectangle of the points, not the closed outline through them. The 2.5-D and slice-by-slice calculators use this test to decide which particles receive a space-charge kick, so particles outside a custom non-rectangular boundary but inside its bounding box are kicked as if inside. For 128 points on a 10 mm circle, the point (9.5, 9.5) mm, 13.44 mm from the centre, is reported inside and receives a horizontal kick of 5.017 μrad in `SpaceChargeCalc2p5D`; the shaped `Boundary2D(..., "Circle", 0.02)` reports it outside and applies none. Rectangular outlines are exact.

title: `BetFreqDep_SC1D_AccNode` cannot be constructed, and its interpolator fails outside the β range
summary: `BetFreqDep_SC1D_AccNode`, the β- and frequency-dependent longitudinal space-charge node, builds its impedance list with `range(self.nbins / 2 - 1)`, which raises `TypeError` in Python 3 for every bin count, so the node cannot be created. Its module's `bilinterp` also fails whenever β lies outside the table: below the range it raises `UnboundLocalError`, and above it indexes the table with a list and raises `TypeError`. The impedance package's copy of `bilinterp` clamps β to the table ends and returns the endpoint value for the same inputs, and `FreqDep_SC1D_AccNode` constructs normally.

title: `addLongitudinalSpaceChargeNode` and `addImpedanceNode` lengthen the lattice for a position outside it
summary: `addLongitudinalSpaceChargeNode(lattice, position, node)` and `addImpedanceNode(lattice, position, node)` search for the drift that contains `position` and, when none does, splice the node and a filler drift in front of the last node instead of raising an error. A position beyond the lattice end or below zero therefore lengthens the lattice silently. Inserting a zero-length node at 5 m into a lattice of three 1 m drifts gives a 6 m lattice (drifts of 1, 1 and 3 m, the node and the original last drift); at −0.5 m the lattice becomes 6.5 m long with the node at 2 m.

title: `SpaceChargeCalc3D.numExtBunches(0)` does not switch off neighbouring-bunch images
summary: `SpaceChargeCalc3D.numExtBunches(n)` forwards n to the solver only when n > 0 and otherwise only returns the current count, so once images of neighbouring bunches are enabled, `numExtBunches(0)` leaves them on and the calculator keeps its periodic, wrapped analysis. A user who sets 2 images and then requests 0 gets 2 back, and an isolated bunch keeps receiving the field of its images; no other method resets the count. For a uniform sphere of radius 1 mm with images every 3.9 mm, a probe's energy kick stays at 0.9339 times the image-free value.

title: `SpaceChargeCalc2p5Drb.setLongAveragingPointsN(n)` with n < 3 makes the energy kicks NaN
summary: `SpaceChargeCalc2p5Drb.setLongAveragingPointsN(n)` accepts any integer, but the longitudinal density derivative is a least-squares quadratic fit over n bins, whose normal equations are singular for n < 3; the determinant is exactly 0 for n = 1 and 2. With n = 2, 1, 0 or a negative value the energy kicks become NaN, or infinite near the bunch ends, without an error, while the transverse kicks stay finite; the default n = 3 and larger values give finite kicks. For a Gaussian bunch of 5000 macroparticles on 16 longitudinal bins, all 5000 energy kicks are NaN with n = 1; with n = 2, 4995 are NaN and 5 are −∞.

title: `SC1D_AccNode` annotates its integer arguments as `float`, and float values terminate the interpreter
summary: `SC1D_AccNode.__init__` annotates `nmacros_min`, `use_sc` and `nbins` as `float` (`BetFreqDep_SC1D_AccNode` does the same for `nmacros_min`), but passes them to the native `LSpaceChargeCalc`, whose argument parser requires integers. A call that follows the annotations, such as `SC1D_AccNode(3.0, 248.0, 1.0, 1.0, 128.0)`, fails argument parsing, and the native error handler ends the process with exit status 1; the error cannot be caught. Any float in one of the three slots, including a NumPy float, does the same, while the same call with integers constructs the node.

title: `TImpedance` kicks each MPI rank's particles with the wake of that rank's particles only
summary: `TImpedance.trackBunch` bins the transverse dipole moments of the bunch (x, x′ and y, y′) along z into arrays that stay local to each MPI rank, and sums over the bunch's communicator only the particle counts, which the kick does not use. Each rank therefore kicks its particles with the wake of its own share of the charge, while the impedance acts on the whole bunch. A rigidly offset bunch spread evenly over 2, 3 and 4 ranks receives 0.5000, 0.3333 and 0.2500 times the kick of the same bunch on one rank, in x and in y. A bunch held entirely on one rank, with the other ranks empty, gets the correct kick.

title: `SpaceChargeCalcSliceBySlice2D` leaves slices without space charge when the bunch communicator lacks some `MPI_COMM_WORLD` ranks
summary: `SpaceChargeCalcSliceBySlice2D.trackBunch` solves the 2-D potential of slice iz only on the rank whose `MPI_COMM_WORLD` rank equals iz modulo the world size, zeroes it on the other ranks, and then sums the potentials over the bunch's own communicator. For a bunch whose communicator lacks some world ranks, set with `setMPIComm`, the slices owned by the missing ranks keep zero potential and the transverse kicks are silently wrong. With two ranks each tracking its own uniform-disk bunch on `MPI_COMM_SELF`, every second of 16 slices is unsolved and the kicks differ from the one-rank kicks by up to 0.7886 of the peak kick. Bunches on `MPI_COMM_WORLD` or a duplicate of it match the one-rank run to 3×10⁻¹⁴.

title: `Bunch.addParticlesTo` writes the source particle attributes onto the target's first rows
summary:
`Bunch.addParticlesTo(target)` appends the source particles to a target bunch with the
same particle attributes, but writes every source attribute value (per-particle `macrosize`, IDs,
initial coordinates) to target rows 0…N−1, N being the number of source particles, instead of to the
appended rows. When the target already holds particles, its first N particles silently take the
source values and the appended particles keep the zero initialization. Merging a two-particle bunch
with weights 100 and 101 into a three-particle bunch with weights 1, 2 and 3 gives weights 100, 101,
3, 0, 0 instead of 1, 2, 3, 100, 101: the total weight drops from 207 to 204 and sits on the wrong
coordinates. Coordinates are appended correctly; an empty target is unaffected.

title: A second `collect_bunch` call overwrites the coordinates returned by the first
summary:
`collect_bunch(bunch, output_dir)` returns, by default, a NumPy memory map backed by a
file whose name depends only on the MPI rank (`collect_bunch_tmpfile_0.dat` on the root). The next
collection into the same directory, by the same process or by another job sharing it (the default is
`/tmp`), reopens that file in write mode, so every array returned earlier silently changes to the
new bunch's coordinates, or to zeros past the new length. Collecting a three-particle bunch with
x = 1, 2, 3 and then one with x = −5, −6, −7 changes the first result to −5, −6, −7; with a
one-particle second bunch it becomes −5, 0, 0. Copies made with `return_memmap=False` are
unaffected.

title: `Bunch.readBunch` drops the last particle when the file does not end with a newline
summary:
`Bunch.readBunch(path)` parses a coordinate line only while the stream has not reached
end-of-file, but reading a final line that lacks a terminating newline already sets that flag. The
last particle of such a file is therefore silently discarded. A three-row file `1 0 0 0 0 0`,
`2 0 0 0 0 0`, `3 0 0 0 0 0` without a final newline loads two particles (x = 1, 2) instead of three,
and a one-row file loads none. Files written by `dumpBunch` end with a newline and are unaffected.

title: `Bunch.readBunch` applies the last row's column count to every row of a read chunk
summary:
`Bunch.readBunch(path)` accepts data rows with six coordinates or with six coordinates
plus the particle-attribute columns, but decides whether to copy attribute columns from the column
count of the last row parsed in each 1000-row chunk. In a file that mixes both widths, a chunk that
ends with a six-column row discards the attribute values of all its full-width rows, and a chunk that
ends with a full-width row gives its six-column rows stale values left in the read buffer by an
earlier read. Appending one six-column row to a `dumpBunch` file whose particles have `macrosize` 5
and 7 reloads both with `macrosize` 0. Files with a single row width are read correctly.

confirmed.scope: stale values for six-column rows in a chunk ending with a full-width row

title: `dumpBunch` writes mass, charge and `macro_size` with six significant digits
summary:
`Bunch.dumpBunch(path)` writes the scalar bunch attributes (mass, charge, `macro_size`
and user doubles) before it sets any output precision, so they carry the stream default of six
significant digits; particle coordinates and attributes are written with eight. A `readBunch`
restart therefore changes the species mass and the macroparticle weight, and the synchronous kinetic
energy is recomputed from the fourteen-digit momentum with the rounded mass. For a 1 GeV proton
bunch with mass 0.93827208816 GeV, the reloaded mass is 0.938272 GeV and the reference kinetic
energy rises by 45.48 eV (4.548×10⁻⁸ relative); `macro_size` 1.23456789×10¹⁰ reloads as
1.23457×10¹⁰.

title: `load_bunch` sets the synchronous-particle position to the saved momentum vector
summary:
`collect_bunch` stores the synchronous particle's momentum vector `pVector()` under
`sync_part["coords"]`, documented as the synchronous particle's coordinates, and `load_bunch` passes
that vector to the position setter `rVector()`, then rebuilds the momentum along z from the kinetic
energy. After a `save_bunch`/`load_bunch` round trip the reference particle therefore sits at the
numerical value of its momentum in metres, and any momentum direction other than z is lost. For a
1 GeV proton reference at the origin moving along z, the reloaded position is (0, 0, 1.696) m
instead of (0, 0, 0); a reference at (0.25, −0.5, 7.0) m tilted by 0.1 rad in x reloads at
(0.1693, 0, 1.688) m with its momentum along z. Kinetic energy and time are restored to double-precision rounding.

title: `Bunch.readBunch` never returns for a missing file
summary:
`Bunch.readBunch(path)` checks the opened stream with `ifstream::bad()`, which stays
false when a file is missing or unreadable, so the open failure is not reported. The coordinate
reader then loops on a stream that never reaches end-of-file: the call spins at full CPU and never
returns, with no message, and a batch job with a misspelled bunch path hangs until its wall-clock
limit. The expected behavior is an immediate error naming the file. The bunch-attribute,
synchronous-particle and particle-attribute readers use the same test and return silently without
reading.

title: `collect_bunch` fails on the root when another MPI rank holds no particles
summary:
`collect_bunch(bunch, output_dir)` has every rank write its local coordinates to a NumPy
memory-map file, then the root reads the other ranks' files as float64. A rank with zero local
particles creates its file through a zero-row memory map, which NumPy stores as a one-byte file; the
root's reader rejects it with "Size of available data is not a multiple of the data-type size".
Collecting or saving a bunch therefore raises `ValueError` whenever any non-root rank is empty, for
example a few particles spread over many ranks or after losses, although the expected result is the
global coordinate array. An empty root rank is handled correctly.

title: Changing the bunch mass leaves the synchronous kinetic energy, β and γ stale
summary:
`Bunch.mass(value)` updates the mass and classical radius but not the synchronous
particle's cached kinetic energy, β and γ, which are recomputed only when its momentum or kinetic
energy is set. The reference keeps its momentum, but `kinEnergy()`, `beta()`, `gamma()` and the maps
that read them keep the old species' values. A default proton bunch set to 2.5 MeV and then given
the H⁻ mass 0.939294 GeV keeps K = 2.500 MeV and β₀ = 0.07285 instead of the 2.497 MeV and 0.07278
its momentum implies, β₀ 0.1083% high. Changed to the electron mass, a 1 GeV proton reference keeps
β₀ = 0.8750 instead of 1.000, and a 1 m TEAPOT drift shifts z of a particle with dE = 1 MeV by
1.577×10⁻⁴ m instead of 5.347×10⁻¹¹ m. Setting the mass first gives consistent values.

title: `ParticleIdNumber.addParticleIdNumbers` reduces over `MPI_COMM_WORLD`, so numbering a bunch on its own communicator hangs
summary: `ParticleIdNumber.addParticleIdNumbers(bunch)` takes the rank, the rank count and an all-reduce of the per-rank particle counts from `MPI_COMM_WORLD`, not from the bunch's communicator, and performs the all-reduce even when `fixedidnumber` makes it unnecessary. A bunch on a sub-communicator or on `MPI_COMM_SELF` therefore cannot be numbered unless every world rank calls the function: a call from the bunch's ranks alone hangs. When every group calls, each group's IDs start after the particle counts of the earlier world ranks, 6–11 for the second of two 6-particle bunches.

confirmed.scope: the hang; the offset identifiers as a contract question

title: Transverse Twiss and dispersion getters return NaN for a bunch without energy spread
summary: `BunchTwissAnalysis.getAlpha`, `getBeta`, `getGamma`, `getDispersion` and `getDispersionDerivative` for x and y remove the energy correlation by dividing by the energy variance ⟨dE²⟩ without the zero check that `getEmittance` has. For a bunch with no energy spread all of them return NaN, `getTwiss` returns NaN for α, β and γ beside a finite emittance, and `computeBunchMoments` returns NaN moments; for 16 particles at x = ±1 mm, x′ = ±0.1 mrad the correct values are α = 0, β = 10.00 m, γ = 0.1000 m⁻¹ and zero dispersion. With the same nonzero dE for every particle, rounding leaves a variance of −7.425e-22 GeV² at dE = 1 MeV, and the bunch reports a dispersion of 0.04205 m instead of 0.

title: `computeBunchMoments` returns zero for the top-order pure-y moment and crashes at orders 0 and 1
summary: `BunchTwissAnalysis.computeBunchMoments(bunch, order, …)` accumulates the moments ⟨(x−⟨x⟩)ⁱ(y−⟨y⟩)ʲ⟩ only for j < order, so the pure-y moment (0, order) is never summed and is returned as 0, and `Moments` and `TeapotMomentsNode` write that zero. For ⟨y²⟩ = 4 mm² and βy = 20 m, the order-2 moment (0, 2) is 0 instead of 2.000e-7 m while (2, 0) is correct, and the order-4 moment (0, 4) is 0 instead of 4.000e-14 m². Without a `macrosize` attribute an order-1 request crashes the interpreter with a segmentation fault, because a missing pair of braces adds a term to the table entry (2, 1) after the loops; an order-0 request writes its first-order entries outside its one-row table and crashes too.

title: Weighted `computeBunchMoments` raises the weights to the moment order and adds an unnormalized copy
summary: With a per-particle `macrosize` attribute, `BunchTwissAnalysis.computeBunchMoments` multiplies the weight w into every power of a particle's offsets, so a moment of order i + j carries wⁱ⁺ʲ, and it adds both the √β-normalized and the unnormalized product before dividing by the total weight once. The weighted central moment Σw(x−⟨x⟩)ⁱ(y−⟨y⟩)ʲ/Σw, divided by βx^(i/2)βy^(j/2), does not change when every weight is scaled, but these values grow with the weight and mix two units. For 32 particles with ⟨x²⟩ = 1 mm² and βx = 10 m, the order-2 moment (2, 0) is 1.000e-7 m without the attribute, 1.100e-6 with weight 1 and 3.300e-6 with weight 3; with weight 1, (4, 0) is 1.010e-12 instead of 1.000e-14 m².

title: Dispersion-subtracted `computeBunchMoments` centers x on the uncorrected mean
summary: `BunchTwissAnalysis.computeBunchMoments(bunch, order, 1, …)`, the setting `TeapotMomentsNode` uses by default, subtracts the dispersive offset D·δ from each particle's x, with D the dispersion and δ the momentum deviation, but centers the result on the plain mean ⟨x⟩: the branch that would compute ⟨x − D·δ⟩ is guarded by a variable that is always zero. Whenever ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 0, (1, 0) reports ⟨x⟩ instead of the betatron centroid and the higher x moments are taken about a centre offset by D⟨δ⟩. For D = 2 m, ⟨δ⟩ = 1.5e-3, βx = 10 m and a 1 mm RMS betatron size, (2, 0) is 1.000e-6 m instead of 1.000e-7 m. Moments of y alone are unaffected.

confirmed.scope: second moment with a mean energy offset

title: `BunchTuneAnalysis` starts with an uninitialized normalization matrix, so a 4×4 normalization leaves the z and dE columns undefined
summary: The `BunchTuneAnalysis` constructor declares a local identity matrix and a local `erase` flag instead of initializing its members, so a new analyzer's normalization matrix holds whatever memory it received. `TeapotTuneAnalysisNode.setNormMatrix` with a 4×4 matrix, used by `setNormMatrixFromBunch` with its default `dim=4` and by `setNormMatrixFromTransferMatrix` for a 4×4 map, writes only the transverse block, so the z and dE columns of the transverse rows keep that memory and enter every normalized coordinate. When the analyzer reuses memory that held −3, a particle advancing by exact tunes 0.2 and 0.3 at actions 1e-7 m and 3e-7 m reports tunes 0.001485 and 0.01832 and actions 5.281e-5 m and 5.614e-5 m. `setNormMatrixFromTwiss` and 6×6 matrices set every element and are unaffected.

title: `setNormMatrixFromBunch(dim=6)` normalizes in dE while the tune analysis applies the matrix to δ
summary: `TeapotTuneAnalysisNode.setNormMatrixFromBunch(bunch, dim=6)` builds the normalization matrix from the bunch covariance in the stored coordinates (x, x′, y, y′, z, dE), but `BunchTuneAnalysis` multiplies the matrix by (x, x′, y, y′, z, δ) with δ = dE/(β₀²E₀) and E₀ the total energy. When x or x′ correlates with z or dE, as with dispersion, the normal modes mix in dE with the wrong scale, so the actions and phases are wrong unless β₀²E₀ = 1 GeV. For a proton bunch with dispersion η = 2 m, betatron emittance 1.000e-7 m and δ = ±1e-3, the mean action of the dispersive mode is 1.213e-7 m at 1 GeV kinetic energy, 3.724e-6 m at 0.1 GeV and 2.648e-7 m at 10 GeV.

title: `addTeapotStatLatsNodeSet` and `addTeapotMomentsNodeSet` label each record with the node entrance but record the state after the node's first part
summary: `addTeapotStatLatsNodeSet(lattice, filename)` and `addTeapotMomentsNodeSet` document one diagnostic "at start of each node" and label each record with the node's entrance position, but they attach the diagnostic as a body child with the default placement, after body part 0. A single-part element is therefore recorded at its exit, a multi-part element after its first part. In a lattice of two 1 m drifts entered with β = 1 m and α = 0, the records labelled s = 0 and s = 1 m report β = 2.000 m and 5.000 m, the values at s = 1 m and 2 m, instead of 1.000 m and 2.000 m.

title: `Bunch.ringwrap` moves particles more than one ring length from the reference to the wrong position
summary: `Bunch.ringwrap(L)` maps a longitudinal coordinate z with |z| > L/2 to −sign(z)·L/2 + fmod(z, L/2), which equals the representative z − L·round(z/L) of z modulo the ring length L only for L/2 < |z| < L. For |z| between L and 3L/2, between 2L and 5L/2, and so on, the result is shifted by half a ring. With L = 20 m, z = 25 m wraps to −5 m instead of 5 m and z = 45 m to −5 m instead of 5 m, a 10 m error. Particles within one ring length of the reference, the case of wrapping on every turn, wrap correctly.

title: `closeStatLats` and `closeMoments` close an unused file handle and leave the records unwritten
summary: `TeapotStatLatsNode(filename)` and `TeapotMomentsNode(filename, order)` open `filename` twice: their `StatLats` or `Moments` helper opens it for appending and writes every record, and the node then opens the same path for writing in a second handle that nothing writes. `closeStatLats()` and `closeMoments()` close only the node's empty handle, so the records stay in the helper's buffer, and the file is empty, or ends at a buffer boundary inside a record, until the helper is garbage-collected or the interpreter exits. After three records and the close call both files have 0 bytes; closing the helper's handle then writes the three records of each.

title: `TeapotTuneAnalysisNode.getData(bunch, index)` rejects every particle index
summary: `TeapotTuneAnalysisNode.getData(bunch, index)` raises "particle index < 0" when `index < bunch.getSize()` holds and "particle index > bunch.getSize() - 1" for every other index, so every integer index raises `ValueError`. The per-particle forms of `getData`, `getTunes` and `getActions` therefore cannot be used; only the all-particle form, with the index omitted, returns data. For a three-particle bunch, indices 0, 1 and 2 raise "particle index < 0" instead of returning that particle's phases, tunes and actions, such as the action 5.000e-8 m of particle 0.

title: `profiles` terminates the interpreter for its documented `xp` and `yp` selectors
summary: `orbit.diagnostics.profiles(bunch, coord, histogram, …)` documents its coordinates as "x[m] xp[rad] y[m] yp[rad] z[m] dE[GeV]" and its error message repeats "x,xp,y,yp,z, or dE", but the code accepts only `x`, `px`, `y`, `py`, `z` and `dE`. Passing `xp` or `yp`, or any other unrecognized name, calls the fatal MPI finalizer, which prints the message and exits the Python process with status 1 instead of returning a histogram or raising an exception. For a five-particle bunch, `xp` and `yp` end the process without writing the histogram file, while `px` and `py` return a grid with sum 5.

title: The `KVDist3D` docstring gives a 100% emittance of eight times the RMS value; the generator produces six
summary: The `KVDist3D` docstring says "100% emittance is 8 times bigger for 3D KV distribution", but the constructor scales each plane's Twiss container by 6 and samples the unit 5-sphere, so the normalized amplitudes satisfy Hx + Hy + Hz = 6 exactly, with H = (u² + (αu + βu′)²)/(βε) and ε the RMS emittance, and no single-plane amplitude exceeds 6. The factor eight belongs to the 3D waterbag, whose docstring states it correctly. A full emittance taken from the docstring overestimates that of the generated KV beam by 33%. For 200000 particles the sum is 6.000000 for every particle and the largest single-plane H is 5.997.

title: The tune-analysis covariance normalization treats a coupled beam as uncoupled when its covariances are below 10⁻⁸
summary: `TeapotTuneAnalysisNode.setNormMatrixFromCovMatrix` and `setNormMatrixFromBunch` choose between plane-by-plane and coupled normalization with `numpy.isclose(off_block, 0.0)`, an absolute tolerance of 10⁻⁸ applied to covariances in m², m·rad and rad². The correct normalization depends on the shape of the beam, not its size, so a beam whose cross-plane covariances are all below 10⁻⁸ is normalized plane by plane however strong its coupling. A matched beam with an x–y coupling rotation of 0.4 rad and eigen-emittances 1 and 2.5 nm·rad gets a normalized covariance whose largest off-diagonal term is 50.72% of the largest diagonal one, and single-turn particle tunes spread over 0.1718–0.8474 and 0.2887–0.5031 instead of the eigentunes 0.2100 and 0.3700. The same beam scaled to 1 and 2.5 µm·rad is normalized exactly.

found.scope: strongly coupled beam, normalized covariance and tunes
tunes of a matched coupled beam

title: `profiles` hangs or aborts an MPI run for a bunch with fewer than two particles or a zero-width coordinate range
summary: `orbit.diagnostics.profiles(bunch, coord, file)` writes a note and returns an empty histogram when the bunch has fewer than two particles or the coordinate range has zero width, but only on rank 0 of the bunch's communicator. The other ranks continue: with fewer than two particles they enter the collective extrema search, which meets a different collective on rank 0, and with a zero-width range they bin on a zero-width grid, where a native fatal error that prints nothing stops them. A `dE` profile of a monoenergetic bunch leaves a two-rank job running after 20 s, and a bunch with 0 or 1 particles aborts it at the next all-reduce with an MPI message-truncated error. On one rank both calls return the empty histogram.

title: Linac Gaussian rotation-error setters give every node the rms angle instead of a random draw
summary: `StraightRotationX_NodesModification`, `StraightRotationY_NodesModification` and `StraightRotationZ_NodesModification.setGaussDistributedAngle(σ, cut_off_level)` draw a truncated Gaussian angle for each linac node and then broadcast and assign σ itself, so every node is rotated by the same angle +σ. A random set of pitch, yaw or roll errors becomes a systematic one. For 200 quadrupoles with σ = 1 mrad and a 3σ cut, all 200 angles are 1.000 mrad, where a Gaussian truncated at 3σ has mean 0 (standard error 0.07 mrad), rms 0.9866 mrad and both signs. The displacement generator of the same module assigns its draws correctly.

title: Yaw and pitch error transforms change the particle energy
summary: The yaw and pitch error transforms (`XSRot`, `YSRot`) of the TEAPOT errors package, also used by the linac rotation-error nodes, rotate (p_x, 1 + δ), with δ = dE/(p₀β₀), as a momentum vector and keep its rotated second component as the new 1 + δ. A frame rotation by an angle a preserves |p| and the energy; here δ changes by sin(a)·p_x + cos(a) − 1 at the entrance, and the exit undoes this only if the element left p_x unchanged. A 1 m quadrupole with k = 2 m⁻², yawed by 1 mrad, changes the energy of a 1 GeV kinetic-energy proton entering at x = 5 mm by 10.15 keV; a yawed 1 m drift shifts a particle with p_x = 2 mrad by Δz = 3.515×10⁻⁷ m. Straight-element rolls and displacements conserve dE.

title: Field sources with a rotated coordinate transform return E and B in the inner frame
summary: `ShiftedFieldSource`, the base of `DipoleFieldSource`, `QuadFieldSource`, `LoopFieldSource` and `MagnetFieldSourceGrid3D`, maps the evaluation point into the source's inner frame with the 4×4 matrix set by `transormfMatrix`. The loops meant to copy its 3×3 rotation block, whose inverse returns E and B to the external frame, use uninitialized counters, and the release build drops them, so the field vector stays in the inner frame. A dipole with inner field (0, 1, 0) T rolled by 0.3 rad returns (0, 1, 0) T instead of (−0.2955, 0.9553, 0) T, and a 1 T/m quadrupole rolled by π/2 returns the field of a quadrupole rolled by π/4, a skew quadrupole, instead of the −1 T/m normal quadrupole. Translations are correct.

title: A collimator or foil node with several parts traverses the whole element in every part
summary: `TeapotCollimatorNode.track` runs once per body part and calls the native collimator over the full collimator length each time. With N parts every particle drifts and scatters over N·L, and the synchronous clock advances N·L/(β₀c), with β₀c the reference speed, while the lattice length stays L. For a 0.5 m node in 4 parts, a particle in the aperture with x′ = 1 mrad starting at 2 mm leaves at 4.000 mm instead of 2.500 mm. A pencil beam in a 5 mm carbon jaw split into 4 parts has the median scattering angle of an unsplit 20 mm jaw, 2.0 to 2.1 times that of the 5 mm jaw. `TeapotFoilNode` crosses its foil N times in the same way.

title: Linac aperture nodes ignore their documented centre offsets c and d
summary: `LinacApertureNode` and its circle, ellipse and rectangle subclasses document c and d as the x and y offsets of the aperture centre, store them, and never pass them to the aperture shape, which stays centred on the axis. A circular linac aperture of radius 10 mm with c = 20 mm and d = −5 mm removes a particle sitting at its centre (20, −5) mm and keeps one on the axis, 20.62 mm from the centre; the TEAPOT `CircleApertureNode` with the same arguments keeps the first and removes the second. Ellipse and rectangle nodes behave the same way; with c = d = 0 the linac and TEAPOT nodes agree.

title: `FieldTracker` bends every species as a particle of charge −1
summary: `FieldTracker` converts the field map's magnetic field to a momentum change with the fixed constant `OrbitConst::charge_electron` = −1 instead of the bunch charge number q, so protons and ions follow the trajectory of a charge −1 particle of the same momentum. In a field with a 0.1 T/m quadrupole gradient over 1 m, a proton of 1 GeV kinetic energy starting 1 mm off axis is defocused to x = 1.009 mm where it should be focused to 0.9912 mm. A q = +2 ion also gives 1.009 mm instead of 0.9824 mm. Reversing the field reverses the kick, so only the charge is ignored.

title: `FieldTracker` computes the momentum as √(E² − (m·K)²), correct only at K = 1 GeV
summary: `FieldTracker` sets the momentum that scales its field kicks to √(E² − (m·K)²), with E the total energy, m the mass and K the kinetic energy in GeV, instead of √(E² − m²). The two agree only at K = 1 GeV, so at other energies particles are bent with the wrong magnetic rigidity. At K = 0.3 GeV a proton-mass particle gets 1.206 GeV/c instead of 0.8081 GeV/c, so its kicks are 0.6701 of their correct size: in a 0.1 T/m quadrupole gradient over 1 m, a charge −1 particle starting 1 mm off axis leaves with x′ = 2.496×10⁻² mrad instead of 3.733×10⁻² mrad. At K = 1.5 GeV the kicks are 1.130 times too strong.

title: Collimator material steps do not advance the longitudinal coordinate
summary: A particle travelling through the material of a `TeapotCollimatorNode` keeps its z, although the synchronous time advances by L/(β₀c) over the collimator length L, with β₀c the reference speed. It arrives without the extra path of its slope and without the lower speed after its energy loss, both of which particles in the aperture get. A 1 GeV proton crossing 0.1 m of carbon at 1% density with x′ = 50 mrad leaves with z = 0 instead of −1.287×10⁻⁴ m. At full density with x′ = 0 the expected mean shift is −3.781×10⁻⁴ m.

title: Linac longitudinal-displacement errors raise NameError; behind it the exit node repeats the entrance shift and the Gaussian setter assigns σ
summary: The linac longitudinal-misalignment path cannot be used. `LongitudinalDisplacementNodesModification()` raises NameError in its constructor, which assigns an undefined `shift_length`, and the error nodes of `ErrorCntrlLongitudinalDisplacement` raise NameError on their first tracked bunch because they pass an undefined `bunc` to `LongDisplacement`. A 1 cm shift should drift the beam by +1 cm at the entrance and −1 cm at the exit, moving a particle with x′ = 1 mrad by 10.00 μm and back. Behind these errors the controller gives the exit node the same +1 cm, so the two drifts add to 2 cm instead of cancelling, and `setGaussDistributedShiftLength` assigns σ to every node instead of the drawn values.

confirmed.scope: NameErrors, exit-node sign and Gaussian setter

title: `MPI_Bcast`, `MPI_Send` and the impedance setters misread or crash on sequences other than lists and tuples
summary: `orbit_mpi.MPI_Bcast`, `MPI_Send`, the group and graph-topology wrappers, and the impedance setters `LImpedance.assignImpedance`, `TImpedance.assignImpedance` and `LSpaceChargeCalc.assignImpedance` accept any Python sequence but read its elements with a macro that is valid only for lists and tuples. Other sequences are read through a tuple's memory layout: broadcasting `range(3)` as `MPI_INT` returns `(3, 1, 3)` instead of `(0, 1, 2)`, and passing a NumPy array to a broadcast, a send or an impedance setter ends the process with a segmentation fault. No Python exception is raised. Lists and tuples work, and `MPI_Allreduce` converts the sequence first and handles NumPy arrays correctly.

title: String `MPI_Bcast` and `MPI_Send` send as many UTF-8 bytes as the string has characters
summary: For `MPI_CHAR` data, `orbit_mpi.MPI_Bcast` and `MPI_Send` take the message length from the Python character count but transmit the string's UTF-8 bytes. A string with non-ASCII characters is longer in bytes than in characters, so its tail is cut: broadcasting `"héllo"` returns `"héll"` on every rank, including the root, and broadcasting `"é"`, `"αβγ"` or `"中文"` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, because the cut falls inside a character. ASCII strings are unaffected.

title: `MPI_INT` all-reduce and broadcast wrap integers outside the 32-bit range
summary: `orbit_mpi.MPI_Allreduce` and `MPI_Bcast` with `MPI_INT` read each Python integer as a C `long` and cast it to a 32-bit `int` without a range check. Values outside −2³¹ … 2³¹ − 1 wrap silently: an all-reduce of 2³¹ returns −2147483648, one of `[2**32 + 5]` returns `(5,)`, and a broadcast of 2³¹ returns −2147483648. Global counts above 2³¹ − 1, such as particle totals summed over ranks, are corrupted without an error, where an `OverflowError` is expected.

title: Serial `MPI_Wtime` returns process CPU time instead of wall-clock time
summary: In builds without MPI, `orbit_mpi.MPI_Wtime()` returns `clock()/CLOCKS_PER_SEC`, the processor time used by the process, whereas MPI defines `MPI_Wtime` as elapsed wall-clock time. Time spent sleeping, waiting or in I/O is missing: across a 0.5 s `time.sleep`, `MPI_Wtime` advances by less than 10⁻⁴ s. Serial timings made with it understate elapsed time by the waiting time, and the same script measures a different quantity on an MPI build. Its intervals track the process CPU time, so they match elapsed time only while the process computes without being descheduled.

title: Integer-list `MPI_Bcast` ends the process on any negative element
summary: Broadcasting a list of integers with `orbit_mpi.MPI_Bcast(..., MPI_INT, ...)` ends the whole process with exit status 1 if any element is negative, printing that the data "is not good". Negative values are valid `MPI_INT` data: a negative scalar broadcasts correctly, as do negative `MPI_DOUBLE` lists and an `MPI_Allreduce` of `[1, -2]`, so broadcasting `[1, -2]` must return `(1, -2)`. The `< 0` test rejects every negative value; a failed conversion, whose error value is −1, is caught only as a side effect.

title: Serial `MPI_Comm_get_name` returns six bytes of an unwritten buffer
summary: In builds without MPI, `orbit_mpi.MPI_Comm_get_name(comm)` returns six bytes of a freshly allocated buffer that nothing writes: the serial stub assigns the text "no mpi" to its local copy of the pointer instead of copying it into the buffer, but reports length 6. The result is arbitrary heap content, so the call usually raises `UnicodeDecodeError` and otherwise returns garbage, where "no mpi" is expected. A shipped space-charge example prints this name. `MPI_Get_processor_name` has the same pointer assignment but reports length 0, so it returns an empty string.

title: `MPI_Group_translate_ranks` returns a list whose first half is `NULL`
summary: `orbit_mpi.MPI_Group_translate_ranks(group_a, ranks, group_b)` creates a list of length n with `PyList_New(n)` and then appends the n translated ranks, so it returns 2n entries whose first n slots are `NULL`. Translating `[0]` within one group prints as `[<NULL>, 0]` instead of `[0]`, and indexing, `list()` or `sorted()` on the result crash the interpreter with a segmentation fault. The wrapper logic is the same with and without MPI.

title: MPI graph-topology wrappers end the process or crash instead of returning results
summary: Three graph-topology wrappers in `orbit_mpi` cannot return a result. `MPI_Graph_get` and `MPI_Graph_neighbors` test the return value of `PyTuple_SetItem` inverted, so the first successfully stored element takes the fatal-error path and ends the process with status 1; `MPI_Graph_get` also sizes its edge tuple by the node count. `MPI_Graph_map` parses five arguments into three output pointers, so calls with three or four arguments end the process and a call with five crashes it with a segmentation fault. In a serial build `MPI_Graph_get(MPI_COMM_WORLD)` exits with status 1 where a pair of tuples is expected; on an MPI build, `MPI_Graph_neighbors` and `MPI_Graph_get` of a two-rank graph communicator exit with status 1 the same way.

found.scope: MPI-build run of the graph wrappers

title: Communicators returned by `MPI_Comm_create`, `MPI_Comm_dup` and `MPI_Comm_split` are never released
summary: The helper that creates the communicator objects returned by `orbit_mpi.MPI_Comm_create`, `MPI_Comm_dup` and `MPI_Comm_split` takes one reference more than it hands out, so these objects are never deallocated: `sys.getrefcount` reports 3 for a communicator held in one variable, where 2 is expected, and each call keeps 24 bytes. Their destructor, which frees the MPI communicator, therefore never runs; only an explicit `comm.free()` releases it. On an MPICH build, a loop that drops `MPI_Comm_dup` results without `free()` aborts the job after 2046 duplicates with "Too many communicators". Each `Bunch` also leaks its 24-byte communicator wrapper; groups from `MPI_Comm_group` are released correctly.

found.scope: communicator exhaustion on an MPI build

title: Native fatal errors exit with status 0
summary: Many native error paths print a fatal-error message and call the no-message finalizer, which ends the interpreter with exit status 0. Requesting a missing bunch attribute with `Bunch.bunchAttrDouble("absent")` prints "Fatal error!" and exits with 0, as do `Boundary2D(4, 4)`, `Grid1D(0, -1.0, 1.0)` and `Grid2D(2, 2)`, whose constructors reject their sizes. Shell scripts, batch schedulers and test harnesses that check the exit status record the failed run as successful. Errors that pass a message to the finalizer exit with status 1; the no-message call is correct only for the deliberate `orbit_mpi.finalize()` stop.

title: `orbitFinalize()` with its default message raises `TypeError`
summary: `orbit.utils.orbitFinalize(message=None)` concatenates the message to a string on rank 0, so calling it with the default argument, with `None` or with a non-string raises `TypeError` before it prints `STOP` and raises `SystemExit(1)`. A caller that relies on the helper to stop the run, or that catches `SystemExit` to handle a stop, sees an unrelated exception instead. With a string message the helper prints it and stops with `SystemExit(1)`.

title: The `USE_MPI` build option advertises `openmpi`, which the build treats as autodetection
summary: The description of the `USE_MPI` Meson option lists `mpich`, `openmpi`, `none` and `auto`, but the build recognizes `ompi` for OpenMPI and sends every other unlisted value to autodetection without a warning. Configuring with `-DUSE_MPI=openmpi` therefore takes the same branch as `-DUSE_MPI=bogus`: it uses MPICH when both libraries are installed and builds without MPI when neither is found, where an explicit request must select OpenMPI or fail. The README lists the correct value `ompi`.

title: MPI wrappers and `Bunch.setMPIComm` accept any Python object as a communicator
summary: `Bunch.setMPIComm` and the `orbit_mpi` functions cast their communicator, datatype and operation arguments to PyORBIT's wrapper structures without checking the Python type. A string is accepted as a bunch communicator and returned by `getMPIComm()`, and in a serial build `MPI_Comm_rank("x")` returns 0 and `MPI_Comm_size(None)` returns 1, with no `TypeError`. In an MPI build the handle is read from the foreign object's memory and passed to MPI: on MPICH, `MPI_Comm_rank("x")`, `MPI_Comm_rank(7)` and `getSizeGlobal()` of a bunch given a string abort the job with "Invalid communicator".

found.scope: MPI-build run of foreign communicator objects

title: `orbit.__version__` reads another distribution's version
summary: `orbit/__init__.py` sets `__version__` from the installed metadata of `ess-python-tools`, an unrelated distribution, instead of `PyORBIT`. Without that package `orbit.__version__` is unset and code that reads it raises `AttributeError`; with it installed, PyORBIT reports that package's version. On an installed source build, `importlib.metadata.version("PyORBIT")` returns the development version while the attribute is unset, and with a synthetic `ess-python-tools` 9.9.9 metadata entry on the path, `orbit.__version__` is "9.9.9". The Sphinx configuration also labels the documentation with an older release, v3.0.1.

title: `from orbit.bunch_utils import *` raises `AttributeError` without NumPy
summary: `orbit.bunch_utils` imports its serialization helpers inside `try/except ImportError`, so that the package loads without NumPy, but always lists them in `__all__`. Without NumPy, `from orbit.bunch_utils import *` therefore raises `AttributeError: module 'orbit.bunch_utils' has no attribute 'collect_bunch'` instead of importing `ParticleIdNumber`; seven of the eight `__all__` names are missing. Named imports such as `from orbit.bunch_utils import ParticleIdNumber` work, and with NumPy installed the star import works.

title: Legacy launcher and build files reference components absent from the repository
summary: Three files in the repository describe build or launch paths that no longer exist. `bin/pyORBIT` runs `python -m orbit.core.pyORBIT`, a module the package does not contain, so it fails at once with an import error. The `Dockerfile` installs Python 2 and runs `make` after sourcing `setupEnvironment.sh`, but the repository has neither that script nor a `Makefile`. `MesonBuild.md` tells users to clone the `meson` branch of a personal fork, which no longer has that branch. The README and the Meson files describe the working build.

title: Docstrings give MeV and volts for quantities the code takes in GeV and GV
summary: `Bunch.mass` is documented as "the mass of particle in MeV" and `SyncPart.kinEnergy` as "kinetic energy of the synchronous particle in MeV", but both are in GeV, as the native comments and the rigidity `B_Rho` assume. `RingRFTEAPOT` documents "Voltages are in Volts", while the ring RF kick adds q·V directly to energies in GeV, so its voltage is in GV. Following the RF docstring with V = 1000 for 1 kV gives an energy kick of 1000 GeV instead of 1.000×10⁻⁶ GeV.

title: A native fatal error on one MPI rank hangs the job while the other ranks wait in a collective, and its message is lost unless the rank is 0
summary: PyORBIT's native fatal errors call `MPI_Finalize` and exit on the failing rank alone; nothing calls `MPI_Abort`. When the other ranks have entered a collective operation, the failing rank blocks in `MPI_Finalize` and the job runs until it is killed. The messages print only on rank 0, and `orbit_mpi.finalize(message)` prints after `MPI_Finalize` returns, so such a job can end or hang with no message at all. In a two-rank job, a missing bunch attribute or `orbit_mpi.finalize(message)` on one rank leaves the job running after 20 s while the other rank waits in an all-reduce; `MPI_Abort` from the same rank ends it at once.

confirmed.scope: the hang while the other ranks wait in a collective, and the lost message

title: Importing `orbit.core` after another component initialized MPI aborts the process, and `orbit_mpi.finalize` fails after another component finalized it
summary: Importing any `orbit.core` module of an MPI build calls `MPI_Init` without asking `MPI_Initialized`; `orbit_mpi.finalize` and the native fatal-error path query the world rank and call `MPI_Finalize` without asking `MPI_Finalized`. A program in which another component has already initialized MPI, such as one that imports `mpi4py` first, therefore aborts at the import with "Cannot call MPI_INIT or MPI_INIT_THREAD more than once", and a `try` block cannot catch it. After another component has finalized MPI, `orbit_mpi.finalize()` ends with status 1 instead of 0 and `finalize(message)` loses its message.

title: Serial `MPI_Recv` reads an uninitialized message size and returns garbage, crashes or stops at random
summary: In builds without MPI, `orbit_mpi.MPI_Recv(type, source, tag, comm)` sizes its result from the serial `MPI_Get_count` stub, which sets the status count but never writes the count it returns, so the wrapper branches on an uninitialized `int`. A serial receive has no sender, and the wrapper's check for a size below 1 makes the intended result a fatal-error stop. Instead the call stops, returns a scalar, returns a tuple of up to hundreds of millions of elements that no one sent, or ends with a segmentation fault, varying from run to run; the tuple holds leftover memory for small sizes and zeros for large ones. Valgrind reports the uninitialized read on every run.
